citation: Philben M; Zhang L; Graham D; Gu B (2020): Mercury Methylation and Soil Organic Matter Degradation in Incubations with Added Acetate, Isotope-Labeled Mercury, and Selective Microbial Inhibitors, Teller and Council Sites, Seward Peninsula, 2018-2019. Next-Generation Ecosystem Experiments (NGEE) Arctic. Dataset. doi:10.5440/1529131

dataset.name: Mercury Methylation and Soil Organic Matter Degradation in Incubations with Added Acetate, Isotope-Labeled Mercury, and Selective Microbial Inhibitors, Teller and Council Sites, Seward Peninsula, 2018-2019
description: This dataset provides the results of laboratory soil microcosm incubation experiments conducted under anaerobic conditions with added acetate, isotope-labeled mercury, and selective microbial inhibitors (2-bromoethanesulfonate and sodium molybdate). The microcosms contained soil collected in August 2018 from the NGEE Arctic Teller Road Site at mile marker 27 (TL_MM27) near Intensive Site 9 (TL_IS_9) and from the Council Road Site (CN_MM71). Incubations were conducted at 8°C for 180 days (Teller incubations) or 60 days (Council incubations). The microcosm headspace was sampled at designated intervals for greenhouse gas concentrations, then destructively harvested and extracted using ultrapure water and 0.1 M KCl for analysis of the porewater geochemistry. This dataset contains one pdf, two csv data files, and one zipped file with raw data.

The Next-Generation Ecosystem Experiments: Arctic (NGEE Arctic), was a research effort to reduce uncertainty in Earth System Models by developing a predictive understanding of carbon-rich Arctic ecosystems and feedbacks to climate. NGEE Arctic was supported by the Department of Energy's Office of Biological and Environmental Research.

The NGEE Arctic project had two field research sites: 1) located within the Arctic polygonal tundra coastal region on the Barrow Environmental Observatory (BEO) and the North Slope near Utqiagvik (Barrow), Alaska and 2) multiple areas on the discontinuous permafrost region of the Seward Peninsula north of Nome, Alaska.

Through observations, experiments, and synthesis with existing datasets, NGEE Arctic provided an enhanced knowledge base for multi-scale modeling and contributed to improved process representation at global pan-Arctic scales within the Department of Energy's Earth system Model (the Energy Exascale Earth System Model, or E3SM), and specifically within the E3SM Land Model component (ELM).

measurementTechnique: Study site and soil collection: Active-layer soil cores were collected from the Teller Road Mile 27 site near Intensive Site 9, and from a thermokarst depression at the Council Road Mile 71, using a gauge auger. The cores were separated into 10-cm segments in the field and shipped to Oak Ridge National Laboratory on ice packs. They were stored frozen until analysis and the start of the incubation experiment. The frozen cores were processed in an anaerobic glove bag. Two 10-cm segments of each core (representing the 20 cm closest to the soil surface) were cut into 0.5 cm3 pieces and thoroughly homogenized using a spoon. 3 g of soil was added to 26 mL serum bottles, and 0.2 mL of one of five amendments was applied: (1) degassed MilliQ water (control); (2) 45 ng/mL 201Hg(II) + 11.34 mg/mL sodium acetate; (3) 45 ng/mL 201Hg(II) + 11.34 mg/mL sodium acetate + 107.143 mM 2-bromoethanesulfonate; (4) 45 ng/mL 201Hg(II) + 11.34 mg/mL sodium acetate +21.43 mM sodium molybdate; and (5) 4.5 ng/mL methyl- 202Hg. For the Council soil only, 225 µmol/mL sodium sulfate was added as a sixth treatment. After the amendment, the microcosms were capped with a thick rubber septum and sealed with an aluminum crimp. The headspace was flushed with N2 for 10 minutes and placed in an 8°C incubator. For the Teller soils, three replicates were constructed for destructive sampling at seven time points for treatments 1 and 2, and three time points for treatments 3, 4, and 5 (69 total microcosms). For the Council soils, three replicates were constructed for sampling at five time points for treatments 1, 2, and 6; at four time points for treatments 3 and 4; and at three time points for treatment 5 (78 total microcosms). Greenhouse gas and chemical analysis: Concentrations of CO2 and CH4 were measured in the headspace of the microcosms prior to destructive sampling, following Roy Chowdhury et al. (2015). 0.5 mL of the headspace was analyzed using an SRI 8610C gas chromatograph with a flame ionization detector (FID). CO2 was converted to CH4 using a methanizer for analysis by FID. Headspace CO2 and CH4 concentrations were converted to total gas production using Henry?s Law based on the temperature of incubation and measured soil pH (Sander, 2015). Soils were destructively sampled and extracted in an anaerobic chamber. 0.75 g of each soil was extracted with 10 mL of degassed MilliQ water or 0.1 M KCl in a 15 mL plastic tube and placed on a reciprocal shaker for 90 minutes. The soil extracts were centrifuged at 3000 RPM for 10 minutes and filtered through a 0.2 µm syringe filter. Aliquots of the KCl extracts were analyzed immediately for pH and ferrous Fe using the 1,10-phenanthroline method (Hach method 8146). The water extracts were analyzed for major anion content, low-molecular weight organic acid concentration, UV-visible absorbance, and water-extractable organic C (WEOC). Samples were either analyzed within three days of collection or frozen until analysis. Anions (Cl-, Br-, NO3-, and SO42-) and organic acids (formate, acetate, propionate, butyrate, and oxalate) were analyzed in the water extracts using ion chromatography following Herndon et al. (2015). The ions were separated using a 4µm Dionex IonPac AS11-HC column and gradient elution. The eluent was 1 mM KOH from 0-7 min, ramping to 15 mM from 7-16 min, 30 mM at 25 min, and 60 mM at 33 min. Ions were detected using a Dionex suppressed conductivity detector. Water-extractable organic carbon (WEOC) concentration in the soil extracts were analyzed using a Shimadzu TOC-L analyzed after acidification with 0.1% HCl. Another 0.75 g of each soil was digested with aqua regia overnight and measured for total mercury on the Lumex analyzer (RA-915+, Ohio Lumex Co., Cleveland, OH). The soil samples were also measured for MeHg. Briefly, ~0.7 g of soil was extracted with 10 mL of 18% (w/v) KBr + 5% (v/v) H2SO4 and 2 mL 1 M CuSO4 in a 50 mL conical centrifuge tube and placed on a reciprocal shaker for 1 h. Meantime, isotope-labeled CH3200Hg was spiked as an internal standard. Afterwards, the mixed soil slurry was extracted with 10 mL methylene chloride and shaken for another 1 h. After extraction, the methylene chloride fraction was transferred with glass pipette into a separate centrifuge tube filled with 20 mL deionized water, which was put inside a water bath and purged with N2 to completely volatilize the methylene chloride and release MeHg into pure aqueous phase. Then the water samples were analyzed using a modified EPA Method 1630, in which MeHg was extracted from the water samples via distillation and ethylation. The extracted MeHg was analyzed with an automated MERX purge and trap system (Brooks Rand, Settle, WA), followed by detection on an inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer (Elan DRC-e, PerkinElmer, Shelton, CT).
